Terezín (Theresienstadt), 1941–1945 · Companion to Victims of Nazi Germany and Holocaust by Country

One hundred and forty-one thousand people.

That many Jews arrived in the walled garrison town of Terezín on regular ghetto transports between November 1941 and April 1945—crushed into quarters built for roughly seven thousand civilians and soldiers—before late-war evacuation marches drove the cumulative total past 150,000; yet on June 23, 1944, outside inspectors spent four to eight hours along painted storefronts and called the place “almost normal.”

Each square stands for 1,000 people in the ghetto cohort. Select any square or ledger line below for primary documentation.

86,934–90,000deported east (only 3,097–3,800 survived)
33,456–35,440died inside Terezín
16,832–17,247registered residents liberated May 1945

Cohort counts follow the USHMM Bohemia & Moravia ledger (141,184 regular arrivals) alongside Yad Vashem and Památník Terezín; see “About these numbers” below.

Eight times over capacity

Before November 1941, Terezín held roughly 3,700 civilian residents and 3,500 garrison soldiers; by July 1942 every non-Jewish resident had been expelled, and by mid-September 1942 daily administrative orders logged between 58,491 and 58,497 prisoners inside a 36-hectare walled perimeter whose actual living quarters measured roughly 95,000 square meters.

That crowding left each prisoner an average of 1.6 square meters of floor space (ranging from 1.5 to 2.0 m² depending on how uninsulated attics and casemates are counted): hunger, cold, enteritis, pneumonia, and typhus killed 3,941 people in September 1942 alone—roughly 131 deaths every day—forcing the construction of a four-furnace crematorium outside the fortress ramparts.

What four to eight hours could—and could not—verify

Under pressure after the deportation of Denmark’s Jews, Nazi authorities spent spring 1944 turning Terezín into a stage set known internally as (“beautification”): first clearing visible overcrowding by deporting 7,503 prisoners to Auschwitz-Birkenau in May, then walking three outside visitors along a choreographed route on June 23, 1944, and filming eleven days of coerced propaganda scenes before shipping 18,402 more people east.

Deportation bars share one zero-based person-count scale (top); the June 23 walkthrough and August–September film shoot sit on their own chronological track below so hours and headcounts are never confused.

What the curated tour displayed

  • A fixed 4-to-8-hour path across freshly painted facades, flower beds, benches, and German civic street signs replacing camp block numbers.
  • Fake shops stocked with confiscated prisoner goods, a mock café, a renovated bank issuing worthless ghetto currency, and a children’s pavilion.
  • Hans Krása’s children’s opera moved into the Sokolovna hall (55th-era ghetto run) alongside staged sports and 36–38 photographs taken by .
  • 2nd Elder , driven in an SS-chauffeured car in top hat and morning coat, reciting scripted remarks while bearing a black eye from Commandant Karl Rahm.

What inspectors never entered—and what followed

  • Unrenovated attics, three-tier barracks off the route, real hospital wards, transport registries, or the adjacent Small Fortress Gestapo prison—where Eppstein was shot Sept 27–28, 1944.
  • Private, unescorted interviews with ordinary residents, or any audit of the 7,503 people shipped to Auschwitz-Birkenau five weeks earlier on Transports Dz, Ea, and Eb.
  • Once ’s 11 days of forced filming ended on September 11, 18,402 people—including Gerron, Krása, and nearly every child performer—were deported to Auschwitz; fewer than 9% survived.

A four-to-eight-hour verdict

Dr. Maurice Rossel’s official International Committee of the Red Cross report (B G 59/12-368.02) described conditions as “almost normal” and accepted Nazi assurances that Terezín was an —a final destination camp with no onward deportations—despite 7,503 people having been shipped to Auschwitz five weeks before his arrival.

Photographs without context

Rossel shot 36 to 38 exposures on his camera (38 archived at the ICRC, roughly 16 prints attached to his report), while German Foreign Office official Eberhard von Thadden circulated the report to neutralize Allied warnings: staged stillness in a single frame looked indistinguishable from normal life.

The film myth, checked

Contrary to postwar lore, the SS propaganda film directed under coercion by was never officially titled “Der Führer schenkt den Juden eine Stadt” (“The Führer Gives the Jews a City”); archival film scholarship confirms that was an ironic prisoner phrase, while the Nazi title was Theresienstadt. Ein Dokumentarfilm aus dem jüdischen Siedlungsgebiet.

I Never Saw Another Butterfly: the children, and one 21-year-old poet

The most repeated sentence about Terezín—“15,000 children passed through, and only about 100 survived”—captures a real catastrophe in blurred arithmetic: archival registries show why the numbers look different depending on whether you count only the children deported east or also those still inside the fortress when Soviet troops arrived.

Children deported east (7,590 youngest cohort): 142 to 245 returned alive (~1.9%–3.2%; over 96% murdered in killing centers)

~7,345–7,448 murdered (>96%)

Inside Terezín & broader youth cutoffs: ~400 died inside Terezín; 1,633 (<15) liberated May 1945 (~half late-war evacuation arrivals); strict <15 totals ~10,500–12,000 while broader youth cohorts (<16/18) approach ~15,000

~400 1,633 <15 youth (<16/18)

Inside the ghetto, Bauhaus-trained artist taught secret art classes to roughly 600 to 660 children—around 550 of whom were later murdered—and before her own deportation to Auschwitz on October 6, 1944, packed two suitcases holding 4,387 children’s drawings now preserved by the Jewish Museum in Prague.

When Hana Volavková edited the anthology I Never Saw Another Butterfly (1959 in Czech; 1964 in English, translated by Jeanne Němcová), it also included typed verse donated after the war: most famously “Motýl” / “The Butterfly,” dated 4. 6. 1942 by —who, contrary to common classroom summaries, was 21 years old when he wrote it in his sixth week in Terezín (37 to 39 days after Transport Ao, six months before Dicker-Brandeis arrived), and who was deported to Auschwitz on September 29, 1944 and murdered at 23.

The Butterfly (tr. Jeanne Němcová)

The last, the very last, So richly, brightly, dazzlingly yellow. Perhaps if the sun’s tears would sing against a white stone. . . . Such, such a yellow Is carried lightly ’way up high. It went away I’m sure because it wished to kiss the world good-bye. For seven weeks I’ve lived in here, Penned up inside this ghetto. But I have found what I love here. The dandelions call to me And the white chestnut branches in the court. Only I never saw another butterfly. That butterfly was the last one. Butterflies don’t live in here, in the ghetto. 4. 6. 1942 Pavel Friedmann

Pavel Friedmann (1921–1944). English translation by Jeanne Němcová from I Never Saw Another Butterfly: Children’s Drawings and Poems from Terezín Concentration Camp, 1942–1944 (© 1978, 1993 Artia, Prague / © 1993 Schocken Books), reproduced in full for non-commercial educational commentary.

Motýl (Czech original, 1942 · Public Domain in CZ/EU)

Ten poslední, ten zcela poslední, tak sytě, hořce, oslnivě žlutý, snad kdyby slunce slzou zazvonilo o bílý kámen... taková, taková žluť vznášel se lehce, tak do vysoka, šel jistě, jistě, chtěl políbit svět svůj poslední. Na sedmý týden tu žiji, ghettoisiert, mí mě tu našli, pampelišky tu na mne volají i bílá větev v dvoře kaštanu. Motýla jsem tu neviděl, ten tenkrát byl poslední. Motýli tady nežijí, v ghettu.

Original Czech text (Jewish Museum in Prague / holocaust.cz); note “na sedmý týden” (“going on the seventh week,” day 37–39 after Transport Ao-956) and 205–230 documented ghetto births vs. ~350 forced abortions.

Home L417 and Vedem: a secret weekly against oblivion

Inside Building L417—a former municipal school converted into a boys’ home holding roughly 300 boys aged 10 to 15 across about ten rooms—the forty to fifty boys of Room 1 formed a self-governing community called the “Republic of Škid” and produced Vedem (“In the Lead”) every Friday night from December 18, 1942 until July 30, 1944.

Only a single master copy of each issue ever existed: the first roughly 30 issues (~190 pages) were typed before typewriter ribbons ran out, and the remaining ~53 issues were written and illustrated by hand on DIN A4 sheets; when the autumn 1944 transports began, 14-year-old contributor hid roughly 800 surviving pages in the blacksmith’s forge behind the Magdeburg Barracks until liberation in May 1945.

Each square stands for 1 of ~100 cumulative boys who lived in Room 1 (1942–1944); sources report ~10 to 15 survivors out of ~92–110 (~9%–16%):

10–15 survived (core + range)
~80–95 murdered

From Vedem · “Rambles through Terezín” #22 (Block E VII – Kavalír Barracks)

EDITORIAL

“Loonie” and “idiot” are the most frequently used terms in the vocabulary of Terezín boys. Lentil soup, youth leader, the hot weather, today’s football match, Madrich, the evening program, liver pate – everything is idiotic. The term loonie is applied to all the above mentioned human beings, including friends, siblings, mothers, and fathers. There is no hypocrisy here: the nine- or fifteen-year-old inhabitant of L 417 will calmly call his friend an idiot. The statement that a proposal, the Madrich’s order, a book written by an Olbracht, a Hostovský, a Poláček, is idiotic, is pronounced in a loud voice, with such certainty and matter-of-factness that it is persuasive. You get used to these two words, and sooner or later they become part of your vocabulary too, along with a number of other Terezín slang words that we shall discuss elsewhere. Loonie and idiot.

But there comes suddenly a sobering-up. You pass a building where faces old and young are pressed against barred windows – loonies. These pale and terrified faces have a common feature; I can’t quite express it – strange faces, but there is one I know and it recognizes me. An older woman starts to laugh hysterically. Her front teeth are missing, she drools disgustingly. She hisses at me, I approach the window, she leans forward and passes me a crumpled, filthy piece of paper. Buy my slippers, buy my slippers, the woman offers in a desperate voice, the woman in whom I have recognized the mother of one of the boys from L 417. Four months ago she was a young, thirty-five-year-old woman, today she is old, gray-haired, toothless. “I’m starving, I’m starving, buy my slippers ...” she pleads, quite hoarse by now. But all I could hear at that moment was the clear, boyish voice of her son, a hundred strong, young voices, crying, “Loonie, Loonie!”

Boys, do you realize that every word has its meaning? You don’t refer to tall people as giants, to toddlers as dwarfs, to blond heads as canaries, to brunets as Schwarters. If you did, they would regard you as – LOONIES! Boys, respect your comrades, respect yourselves. You are responsible not only for your actions, but also for your words. Every one of your mothers may one day have to sell slippers made of crumpled paper from behind the barred windows of the madhouse.

— · Preserved in Archiv Památníku Terezín (ID A 1317), published at vedem-terezin.cz (copyright retained by Památník Terezín; reproduced for non-commercial educational commentary, with three minor HTML encoding typos cleaned silently for readability).

What one tour—and one frame—cannot see

Genocide never asks the outside world to look at the whole ledger; it offers one curated street, one guided afternoon, one photograph of smiling children on a bench, or one reel of rehearsed film, and dares observers to mistake a stage-managed corridor for life inside a sealed perimeter.

That is why a single video, a single photograph, or a single escorted walkthrough in person can never verify what is happening on the ground: only sustained, independent documentation—the transport manifests, the body counts in the barracks, the 4,387 hidden drawings, and the 800 clandestine pages that boys risked their lives to write and bury—measures a crime for which there can be no forgiveness.

What outside inspection relied on (1944)

  • 1 escorted visit: 4–8 hours along freshly repainted streets on June 23, 1944.
  • 36–38 photographs: snapped along the approved path (~16 attached to Rossel’s report).
  • 11 filming days: coerced scenes (Theresienstadt, Aug–Sep 1944), ~20 minutes surviving.
  • 1 forced statement: Elder Paul Eppstein speaking from an SS car with a bruised face, shot three months later.

What ground-level archives prove (1941–1945)

  • 140,000–141,184 regular arrivals (150,000–155,000+ with 1945 evacuees) in quarters built for ~7,000–7,200.
  • 33,456–35,440 dead inside Terezín (3,941 in September 1942 alone) + 86,934–90,000 deported east across ~63 transports.
  • 7,590 youngest children deported east (only 142–245 returned alive) + ~10–15 survivors among ~92–110 Room 1 boys.
  • 4,387 drawings preserved in two suitcases + ~800 Vedem pages hidden in a smithy.

About these numbers, sources & licensing

  • Why regular arrivals and total arrivals differ: USHMM’s Bohemia & Moravia ledger counts 141,184 regular ghetto arrivals (Nov 1941–Apr 1945), matching ~140,000 in USHMM, Yad Vashem, and Památník Terezín summaries; adding ~13,000–15,000 concentration camp evacuees driven into Terezín in April–May 1945 raises the total to 150,000–155,000+ and raises May 1945 liberation counts from 16,832–17,247 registered residents to roughly 30,000.
  • Why Terezín death and deportation numbers appear as ranges: USHMM’s wartime ledger lists 33,456 deaths inside Terezín; Yad Vashem (35,440) and Památník Terezín (>35,000) include late-war evacuation and May–June 1945 typhus epidemic deaths. Eastern deportees span 86,934 (Yad Vashem Timeline) to 88,202 (USHMM ledger) to ~90,000, with 3,097–3,800 survivors.
  • Untangling “15,000 children / ~100 survived”: Památník Terezín records 7,590 youngest children deported east with 142 survivors (broader cohorts give 242–245), omitting the 1,633 children under 15 liberated inside Terezín in May 1945 (roughly half long-term inmates, half late-war evacuation arrivals) and ~400 in-ghetto child deaths; strict <15 totals run ~10,500–12,000 while broader youth cutoffs reach ~15,000.
  • Room 1 (Vedem) & 1944 inspection nuances: Room 1 survivor estimates reflect Kurt Kotouč’s oral approximation (~10 of 100–110) alongside compiled tallies (15 of ~100 or 15 of 92 contributors). June 23 visit durations (4 hours at holocaust.cz vs. 6–8 hours at USHMM) reflect guided-route hours vs. total on-site itinerary; ICRC archives catalog 38 Rossel photographs vs. 36 cited in Farré & Schubert (2009).
  • Copyright, attribution & open licenses: Fonts (Spectral and Public Sans) are open-licensed under the SIL Open Font License and embedded offline via tools/embed_fonts.py. Bedřich Fritta drawings, the February 1944 Red Cross map (Jewish Museum in Prague), and Walter Scheiwiller’s February 11, 1945 USHMM photos (pa1121409, pa1121419) are Public Domain; Building L417 and Magdeburg Barracks photos are used under CC BY-SA 3.0 and CC BY-SA 2.0 DE with photographer credit above.
